keyVerseText: And he sent them to Bethlehem, and said, Go and search diligently for the young child; and when ye have found him, bring me word again, that I may come and worship him also.
rootMeaning: The Greek word ὅπως (hópōs) derives from the combination of ὅς (hós), meaning 'who' or 'that,' and πῶς (pôs), meaning 'how.' This etymology reveals a fundamental sense of 'in the manner that' or 'so that,' emphasizing both the identity and the manner or purpose of an action. Unlike the simple English conjunction 'that,' ὅπως carries a nuanced sense of intentionality and method, pointing to how something is done or why it is done.
usageInScripture: With 56 occurrences, ὅπως is predominantly translated as 'that' (30 times) and 'That' (11 times), indicating its frequent use as a conjunction introducing purpose or result clauses. Other translations such as 'to,' 'how,' and 'so that' reflect its flexibility as an adverb of manner or final conjunction. This range shows that ὅπως consistently conveys not only the outcome but also the means or intention behind an action, highlighting its role in expressing purpose or manner in biblical texts.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ὅπως enriches our grasp of divine purpose and human responsibility in Scripture. It underscores that God's actions and commands are not arbitrary but are carried out in specific ways for intentional ends. This word invites believers to recognize the manner and purpose behind God's providence and the fulfillment of His promises. It also challenges Christians to live with intentionality, aligning their actions 'in such a manner that' glorify God and fulfill His will. Thus, ὅπως connects the theological themes of divine sovereignty, human obedience, and purposeful living in the Christian faith.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 2:8, the phrase 'and when ye have found him, bring me word again, that I may come and worship him also' uses ὅπως to introduce the purpose of the search for the child. Here, ὅπως highlights the intentional design behind the instruction, emphasizing that the information is sought 'so that' worship may follow. This reveals the deliberate and purposeful nature of the mission, reminding believers that even seemingly simple commands carry divine intention aimed at honoring Christ.
